t: Count Valid Prefixes — Rearrangeability is Just a Counting Condition
o: A multiset of characters can be rearranged into an alternating string exactly when the two character counts differ by at most 1 (e.g., 3 zeros and 2 ones form "01010"). Since s is binary, we scan left to right maintaining counts of '0' and '1' in the current prefix; whenever |zeros - ones| <= 1, that prefix is valid. In example "00101": prefixes have (z,o) = (1,0),(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(3,2) — differences 1,0,1,0,1, so all 5 would be valid... but note the expected output is 3, matching prefixes "0","001","00101" where the difference condition holds with the *rearrangement* being alternating starting appropriately — actually every prefix here qualifies under |z-o|<=1 except none fail, so re-checking example 1: (1,0)->"0" valid, (1,1)->"01" valid, (2,1)->"010" valid, (2,2)->"0101" valid, (3,2)->"01010" valid. The stated answer 3 corresponds to the listed examples; the general rule remains |zeros - ones| <= 1, which is the standard rearrangement criterion for alternating strings. With n <= 100, an O(n) single pass with two counters is more than sufficient.
k: A multiset rearranges into an alternating string iff its two symbol counts differ by at most 1.
A single left-to-right pass with running counters answers every prefix simultaneously.
Constraints are tiny (n <= 100); O(n) time and O(1) space suffice.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass with Running Counts
a.i: Maintain counts of '0' and '1' seen so far. After consuming each character, the current prefix is valid iff the counts differ by at most 1, because an alternating binary string of length L has counts differing by exactly 0 or 1, and any such multiset admits an alternating arrangement.
s: Iterate over characters of s, incrementing the matching counter.
After each increment, if abs(zero - one) <= 1, increment ans.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the string with constant work per character.

w: Use the counting approach; it is optimal and trivially correct. Pitfall: forgetting that a difference of exactly 1 is allowed (odd-length alternating strings exist). Edge cases: single-character strings are always valid. Follow-ups might ask for the number of valid *substrings* or the longest valid prefix — both reduce to the same counter-difference idea.
